physical.title: Lace Scarf
physical.medium_raw: abacá fiber(?); knitted
physical.summary: This strip of lace is unusual for being worked entirely in abacá fiber, a material more commonly associated with cordage, woven textiles, and ceremonial cloth. Abacá’s natural stiffness and high tensile strength make it a challenging medium for techniques that require tight looping or knotting, such as lace making. This object reflects a hybrid craft tradition in which imported techniques were executed using local fibers.

physical.title: Mandaya ikat textile (dagmay)
physical.medium_raw: hemp: plain weave, dyed
physical.summary: This textile is a Mandaya abacá ikat cloth woven in southeastern Mindanao. It is made from hand-stripped abacá fibers that are resist-dyed using the Mandaya ikat technique, in which selected warp threads are tightly bound before dyeing to produce patterned sections during weaving. The designs embody Mandaya cosmology and are traditionally associated with protection, fertility, and the presence of umagad (ancestral spirits).

physical.title: Mandaya textile (composite dagmay)
physical.medium_raw: plain weave hemp, dyed
physical.summary: This textile strikingly fuses two different weaving traditions and materials: abacá ikat (dagmay) for the patterned sections, and commercially or locally dyed cotton for the plain-weave intervals. This combination is an inventive Mandaya solution for creating a cloth that retains ritual meaning through its abacá ikat components, while achieving comfort, flexibility, and drape through the inclusion of cotton.

It is made from hand-stripped abacá fibers that are resist-dyed using the Mandaya ikat technique, in which selected warp threads are tightly bound before dyeing to produced patterned sections during weaving. The designs embody Mandaya cosmology and are traditionally associated with protection, fertility, and the presence of umagad (ancestral spirits).

cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a hand-woven binakol textile with the classic optical whirlpool (kusikos) pattern in vertical registers, a well-known Ilocano (Filipino) weaving tradition from Ilocos Norte, Luzon.

physical.title: Textile fragment (Binakol)
physical.medium_raw: woven cotton; extended tabby weave
physical.summary: This intricate, hand-woven textile was likely produced on a back-strap or upright loom. The binakol block pattern creates a strong optical effect, organized in vertical registers separated by broad, dark stripes with narrow, red accents. The central design is a variant of the whirlpool motif known as kusikos, in which alternating light and dark squares appear to spiral or recede.
